transcript: Okay, initial evaluation for Rosalind Achterberg, right shoulder. Chief complaint is right shoulder pain and, um, difficulty lifting the arm overhead. Onset was about seven weeks ago, gradual, no specific injury that she can recall, and it's been getting worse. Prior treatment, she saw her primary care doctor, x-ray was negative, referred to outpatient PT with a diagnosis of right rotator cuff tendinopathy. Past medical history, hypertension and type two diabetes. Surgical history, appendectomy in, uh, in her twenties. Current medications, lisinopril ten milligrams daily, metformin five hundred milligrams twice a day, and ibuprofen as needed for pain. No known drug allergies. Alert and oriented. No falls in the past year. Prior level of function fully independent, she works part time as a cashier. Lives in a single story home with her husband. Her goals are to reach the overhead cabinets and sleep on her right side. Pain is worst seven out of ten, best two out of ten, currently four out of ten. QuickDASH score fifty two. Right hand dominant. Posture shows forward head and rounded shoulders. Right shoulder active flexion one hundred ten degrees, abduction ninety degrees, external rotation forty degrees, left side is full. Strength, right shoulder flexion four minus out of five, abduction three plus out of five, external rotation four out of five. Gait is normal, no assistive device. Hawkins-Kennedy positive, empty can test positive. Assessment is right rotator cuff tendinopathy limiting overhead function, presentation is evolving, skilled PT is medically necessary. Educated on activity modification and a home program. Rehab potential is good. Precaution, no lifting over ten pounds overhead. Short term goal, flexion to one hundred forty degrees in three weeks. Long term goal, full overhead reaching in six weeks. Plan is twice a week for six weeks, certification period starts today for sixty days.

transcript: Follow up visit for Rosalind Achterberg, right shoulder, week three. She reports the pain is better, down to three out of ten at rest and five out of ten with overhead reaching. She says she slept on that side two nights this week which is new. We did therapeutic exercise for twenty minutes, scapular retraction, isometric external rotation at the doorway, and wall slides. Then manual therapy fifteen minutes, posterior capsule stretching and soft tissue mobilization to the upper trapezius and, uh, and the infraspinatus. Right shoulder active flexion is now one hundred thirty degrees, abduction one hundred five degrees, external rotation fifty degrees. Strength right shoulder abduction four minus out of five, external rotation four out of five. Response to treatment was good, no increase in symptoms afterward. Functional status, she can reach the second shelf now but still not the overhead cabinet. Short term goal of flexion to one hundred forty degrees is not met yet but she is close. Plan, continue twice a week, progress to light resistance band work next visit.

transcript: Initial evaluation, Desmond Okonkwo-Reyes, left shoulder. Chief complaint is left shoulder stiffness and pain, he says it feels like the arm is stuck. Onset gradual about five months ago, no injury. He was referred by his endocrinologist with a diagnosis of left adhesive capsulitis. Past medical history, type two diabetes for twelve years, hypothyroidism, and, um, high cholesterol. Medications are metformin one thousand milligrams twice daily, levothyroxine one hundred micrograms daily, and atorvastatin twenty milligrams at bedtime. Allergies, no known drug allergies except, uh, except sulfa. Lives alone in a second floor apartment with stairs, no elevator. Works as a delivery driver, currently on modified duty. Prior level of function independent. Goals are to reach behind his back to get his wallet and to lift boxes at work again. Pain worst eight out of ten, best three out of ten, current six out of ten. Left shoulder active flexion eighty degrees, abduction seventy degrees, external rotation fifteen degrees, internal rotation to the back pocket only. Passive range is similarly limited which is consistent with capsular restriction. Strength testing limited by pain, flexion four minus out of five, abduction four minus out of five. Alert and oriented, no falls. Assessment is left adhesive capsulitis in the freezing stage with significant capsular restriction and functional loss, complicated by long standing diabetes. Skilled PT medically necessary. Rehab potential good but expect a prolonged course. Short term goal, external rotation to thirty degrees in four weeks. Long term goal, functional overhead reach and hand behind back in twelve weeks. Plan, three times a week for twelve weeks. Certification period sixty days.

transcript: Follow up for Desmond Okonkwo-Reyes, left shoulder, week five. He reports the night pain is finally easing, four out of ten at rest, six out of ten with end range stretching. Treatments today, manual therapy twenty minutes, joint mobilization grade three at the glenohumeral joint in the, uh, in the anterior and inferior directions, plus posterior capsule stretch. Therapeutic exercise fifteen minutes, pulley for flexion, table slides, and external rotation with a stick. Neuromuscular re-education ten minutes for scapulohumeral rhythm retraining with tactile cueing at the scapula. Left shoulder active flexion one hundred degrees now, abduction ninety degrees, external rotation twenty five degrees. Strength flexion four out of five. Response to treatment good, he tolerated the mobilizations well. Functional status, he can now reach the back pocket and get his wallet which was one of his goals. Short term goal of external rotation to thirty degrees is not met, he is at twenty five. Plan, continue three times a week, add capsular stretching to the home program.

diagnosis: S/P right rotator cuff repair (arthroscopic, supraspinatus)
transcript: Okay this is Ingrid Vasquez-Thornbury, eight weeks out from her right rotator cuff repair, arthroscopic supraspinatus. She says the shoulder feels stronger this week, pain is two out of ten at rest and four out of ten with resisted motion. Still in the sling for community outings only. We did therapeutic exercise twenty five minutes, active assisted flexion in supine, isometrics into external rotation and abduction, and scapular stabilization. Manual therapy fifteen minutes, scar mobilization at the portal sites and gentle glenohumeral joint mobilization. Then ultrasound eight minutes to the anterior shoulder at one point five watts per centimeter squared for pain and tissue extensibility. Right shoulder active flexion one hundred twenty degrees, abduction one hundred degrees, external rotation thirty five degrees. Strength flexion three plus out of five to four minus out of five, external rotation three plus out of five. Response to treatment was good. Precautions still in effect, no active internal rotation behind the back and no lifting over five pounds per the surgeon's protocol. Functional status, she is independent with dressing and grooming, still needs help with overhead reaching at home. Short term goal of active flexion to one hundred twenty degrees is met today. Plan is continue twice a week for six more weeks and begin light resistance next visit.

transcript: Follow up, Barnaby Quillfeather, left shoulder impingement, week two. He reports pain with overhead work as a painter, five out of ten with activity, one out of ten at rest. Was that better than last week, yes, definitely better. Today we did therapeutic exercise eighteen minutes, rotator cuff strengthening with a yellow band, scapular setting, and prone horizontal abduction. Therapeutic activities fifteen minutes, simulated overhead painting task with a light roller working on scapulohumeral mechanics and pacing. Electrical stimulation twelve minutes to the left upper trapezius for pain modulation. Left shoulder active flexion one hundred fifty degrees, abduction one hundred forty degrees, external rotation fifty five degrees. Strength abduction four out of five, external rotation four out of five. Neer test still mildly positive. Response to treatment good. Functional status, he can work overhead for about twenty minutes before symptoms start, up from ten minutes at evaluation. Plan, continue twice a week for four more weeks and progress the resistance band to red.

transcript: This is Marisol Fitzgerald-Nakamura, ten weeks post left SLAP repair, type two labral tear. She is a recreational swimmer and wants to get back in the pool. Pain is one out of ten at rest, three out of ten with end range external rotation. Treatments, therapeutic exercise twenty two minutes including prone Y and T raises, external rotation at ninety degrees abduction with a light band, and rhythmic stabilization. Neuromuscular re-education fifteen minutes for proprioceptive training with the shoulder in the overhead position and closed chain work on the wall. Left shoulder active flexion one hundred sixty degrees, abduction one hundred fifty five degrees, external rotation at ninety degrees abduction is seventy degrees. Strength external rotation four out of five, internal rotation four plus out of five. Response to treatment was good, no apprehension with the overhead position today which is an improvement. Precaution, no aggressive biceps loading until twelve weeks per protocol. Functional status independent with all activities of daily living, not yet cleared for swimming. Long term goal of return to lap swimming remains in progress. Plan, continue twice a week and initiate a return to swim progression at twelve weeks.

diagnosis: S/P left reverse total shoulder arthroplasty
transcript: Alright, this is the initial physical therapy evaluation for Cornelius Adebayo-Whitlock, he is four weeks out from a left reverse total shoulder arthroplasty. Referral is from his orthopedic surgeon with the diagnosis of status post left reverse total shoulder arthroplasty and the referral asks for evaluation and treatment per the reverse total shoulder protocol. Chief complaint, he says the shoulder is sore and very weak and he cannot use the arm for anything functional yet. He also mentions some, um, some stiffness in the elbow from being in the sling. History of present illness, he had increasing left shoulder pain for about four years, was diagnosed with rotator cuff arthropathy, had a subacromial injection about two years ago that helped for a few months, and then the pain became constant and he lost the ability to lift the arm at all. Surgery was performed four weeks ago, uneventful per the operative report, and he was in a sling full time for the first three weeks and is now weaning out of it during the day. Date of onset of the current episode is the surgical date, four weeks ago. Mechanism is surgical, not traumatic. Course since onset, he says the incisional pain is much better than the first week but the weakness has not changed. Prior treatment includes the injection I mentioned, and about six visits of physical therapy two years ago which he says did not help much. Past medical history is significant, he has atrial fibrillation, he has hypertension, he has type two diabetes, he has chronic kidney disease stage three, he has osteoarthritis in both knees, and he had a transient ischemic attack about six years ago with no residual deficits. Surgical history, left reverse total shoulder arthroplasty four weeks ago, right knee arthroscopy about fifteen years ago, and a cholecystectomy in his forties. Current medications, and this is a long list, he takes apixaban five milligrams twice a day, metoprolol twenty five milligrams twice a day, lisinopril twenty milligrams daily, metformin one thousand milligrams twice a day, atorvastatin forty milligrams at bedtime, furosemide twenty milligrams daily, allopurinol three hundred milligrams daily, acetaminophen one thousand milligrams three times a day as needed for pain, oxycodone five milligrams as needed which he says he only takes at night now, a daily multivitamin, and vitamin D two thousand units daily. Allergies, he is allergic to penicillin, and he says it gives him a rash. Cognition, he is alert and oriented to person place and time, follows multi step instructions without difficulty. History of falls, he reports one fall about eight months ago in the bathroom, no injury, and he denies any falls since surgery. Does he worry about falling, yes, somewhat, particularly on stairs. Social history and living environment, he lives with his wife in a two story home, the bedroom and full bathroom are upstairs, there are fourteen steps with a rail on the right going up. He is retired, he was a high school science teacher. He drives but has not driven since surgery. His wife is assisting with dressing and bathing currently. Code status is full code. Prior level of function, before surgery he was independent with all activities of daily living although he had stopped doing anything overhead with the left arm for over a year. He walked about a mile a day for exercise. Patient goals, he wants to be able to dress himself independently, reach a shelf at shoulder height, and get back to his daily walks. Pain, worst is six out of ten, best is one out of ten, current is three out of ten. The pain is described as a deep ache in the anterior shoulder, worse at night and with any attempt at active elevation. Outcome measurement tool, we administered the QuickDASH and his score is seventy one. Handedness, he is right hand dominant, so this is his non dominant arm. Posture, he presents with a protective posture, elevated and protracted left scapula, forward head, and rounded shoulders bilaterally. Range of motion, left shoulder passive flexion is ninety degrees, passive abduction is eighty five degrees, passive external rotation is twenty degrees with the arm at the side. Active flexion is forty degrees, active abduction is thirty five degrees, active external rotation is ten degrees. Right shoulder is within normal limits throughout. Left elbow flexion is one hundred thirty degrees and extension lacks ten degrees, which is that stiffness he mentioned from the sling. Strength, left shoulder flexion is two plus out of five, abduction is two plus out of five, external rotation is two out of five, and internal rotation is three out of five. Left elbow flexion four out of five, extension four out of five, grip strength is grossly four plus out of five and symmetric to the right. Functional mobility and gait, he ambulates independently without an assistive device, gait is unremarkable, he negotiated four steps with one rail using a step to pattern and needed no physical assistance. Community mobility was not tested today. Special tests were deferred given the recent arthroplasty. Skin, the incision is well approximated with steri strips intact, no drainage, no erythema. Assessment and clinical impression, this is a sixty eight year old man four weeks status post left reverse total shoulder arthroplasty presenting with significant active range of motion and strength deficits in the left upper extremity, consistent with the expected post operative course for a reverse total shoulder. Clinical complexity is high given the multiple comorbidities, the anticoagulation, and the two story living situation. Justification for skilled care, he requires skilled physical therapy for protocol guided progression of passive to active assisted to active range of motion, deltoid retraining which is the primary elevator after a reverse total shoulder, scapular mechanics, and safe functional reintegration. Rehab potential is good although the comorbidities may slow progress. Patient education, we reviewed the reverse total shoulder precautions in detail, reviewed the home exercise program, and discussed activity pacing. Precautions, no active internal rotation behind the back, no shoulder extension past neutral, no weight bearing through the left upper extremity, and no lifting greater than two pounds until cleared by the surgeon at twelve weeks. Participation, he was highly engaged and his wife attended and was educated as well. Short term goals, first, increase left shoulder active flexion to ninety degrees in four weeks. Second, independent with the home exercise program in two weeks. Third, independent with upper body dressing in four weeks. Long term goals, first, left shoulder active flexion to one hundred twenty degrees in twelve weeks. Second, left shoulder strength four out of five in twelve weeks. Third, return to independent community ambulation and daily walks in eight weeks. Plan of treatment, frequency is two times per week, duration is twelve weeks, intensity is forty five minutes per session. Discharge and transition plan, we anticipate discharge to a home exercise program with follow up with the surgeon at twelve weeks. Certification period begins today and runs for sixty days. Interventions planned include therapeutic exercise, neuromuscular re-education for deltoid retraining, manual therapy for the elbow and scapula, and therapeutic activities for functional reintegration. Let me go back and add some more detail on the systems review. Cardiopulmonary, he denies chest pain and denies shortness of breath at rest, he does report mild exertional dyspnea when walking up the fourteen steps at home, which he says has been present for about a year and has been evaluated by his cardiologist. Resting heart rate today was irregular which is consistent with his known atrial fibrillation. He denies dizziness and denies palpitations today. Integumentary, aside from the surgical incision the skin is intact throughout the left upper extremity, no rashes and no open areas. I did note mild dependent edema in the left hand and forearm, circumferential measurement at the wrist was seventeen centimeters on the left compared to sixteen centimeters on the right, so about a one centimeter difference which is likely positional from the sling. Palpation, he has tenderness over the anterior deltoid and over the incision itself, and he has significant guarding and hypertonicity in the left upper trapezius and levator scapulae, which is consistent with the compensatory shrugging pattern I observed. No tenderness over the cervical spine. Cervical screen, cervical active range of motion is functional in all planes, rotation is about sixty degrees bilaterally, and cervical motion does not reproduce his shoulder symptoms, so I am not implicating the cervical spine as a pain generator here. Neurological screen, sensation is intact to light touch throughout the left upper extremity in all dermatomes, he denies any numbness or tingling, deep tendon reflexes were not formally tested today. Let me also talk about his sleep because it is a significant functional limitation. He reports he is sleeping in a recliner and has been since the surgery, he wakes about three times a night, and he says the night pain is the worst part of this whole thing. He has tried sleeping flat in the bed twice and could not tolerate it. More on his prior imaging, he brought a copy of the pre operative report, the x-ray showed superior migration of the humeral head with glenohumeral joint space narrowing and the MRI from about three years ago showed a massive full thickness tear of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus with grade three fatty infiltration, which is of course why he went to a reverse rather than a repair. Additional functional detail on activities of daily living. Upper body dressing, he requires moderate assistance from his wife for pulling a shirt over the head, he can manage a button down shirt with setup only. Lower body dressing he is independent. Bathing, he requires assistance to wash the right axilla and the back, contact guard for tub transfer. Grooming he is independent using the right hand. Toileting independent. Feeding independent. Meal preparation, his wife is doing all of it currently, he says he was doing about half of the cooking before surgery. He is not managing his own medications, his wife sets them up in a weekly organizer, and that was true before surgery as well so that is not a change. Household mobility he is independent, he negotiates the fourteen steps to the bedroom once in the morning and once at night and he says he holds the rail with the right hand and takes it slowly. Now let me describe the home exercise program I issued today. I gave him four exercises. Pendulum exercises, ten circles each direction, three times a day. Passive supine flexion using the right arm to assist the left, ten repetitions holding five seconds, three times a day. Active elbow flexion and extension to address that elbow stiffness, fifteen repetitions, three times a day. And scapular retraction in sitting, ten repetitions holding three seconds, twice a day. He returned demonstration on all four and performed them correctly with verbal cueing only on the supine flexion. His wife was also instructed and returned demonstration on assisting with the supine flexion. I gave them a printed handout with photographs. Regarding the protocol progression I discussed with him, phase one which is weeks zero to six is passive and active assisted range of motion only with the precautions we discussed, phase two which is weeks six to twelve adds active range of motion and begins deltoid strengthening, and phase three which is after twelve weeks adds progressive resistance. I explained that with a reverse total shoulder the deltoid becomes the primary elevator because the rotator cuff is deficient, and that is why the deltoid retraining is such a central part of what we are going to do. He verbalized understanding and asked good questions about when he could drive again, and I told him that is a decision for his surgeon but that it is typically around six to eight weeks. One more thing on the goals, I want to add a fourth short term goal, which is that he will sleep in the bed rather than the recliner for at least four nights per week within six weeks, because the sleep disruption is genuinely affecting his recovery. And a fourth long term goal, independent with upper body dressing without assistance from his wife by twelve weeks. Barriers to discharge, the two story home with the bedroom upstairs is the main environmental barrier, and the anticoagulation means we need to be careful with aggressive manual techniques given the bruising risk. Facilitators are that he is highly motivated, cognitively intact, and has a supportive spouse who attended today. I will let the office assign the codes.
